title: Drought delivers ‘worst case scenario’ for fire scar recovery in Wyoming’s Bighorn Basin
description:
At the front end of what’s shaping up to be another active fire year, landowners and rangeland specialists speak to the challenges of healing a landscape burned over by the Red Canyon Fire. 
The post Drought delivers ‘worst case scenario’ for fire scar recovery in Wyoming’s Bighorn Basin appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
HOT SPRINGS COUNTY—As Derek Trauntvein traveled around the Bighorn Basin for his job with the new U.S. Wildland Fire Service this spring, the landscape looked so desiccated and browned out that it resembled late summer conditions.
“In a normal year, this would be lush green right now,” Trauntvein told a gathering of journalists last week in the 195-square-mile scar of 2025’s Red Canyon Fire. “June is the best time to visit the Bighorn Basin, because it’s green and beautiful.” 
Not so in 2026. 
On the heels of the warmest winter ever, which coincided with the sparsest spring snowpack on record, the normal green-up is absent, he said. 
“Green-up is delayed, and in some places not even happening,” Trauntvein said. 
An unburned tract of sagebrush-steppe rangeland just south of the Red Canyon Fire, which quickly burned up nearly 125,000 acres of the Hot Springs County in summer 2025. (Hannah Nikonow/Intermountain West Joint Venture)
Measured moisture levels in the basin’s vegetation are at a July-like level, an indication that fire season’s probably going to come early.
“We may not grow anything to burn,” Trauntvein said, “but we still have a lot of residual [vegetation] from last year, and that’s definitely going to be problematic for this coming summer.” 
The Bighorn Mountains foothills “look like August right now” and the cheatgrass he’s spotted is already drying out and especially concerning. When a cheatgrass-infested area burns and the nonnative grass dominates the fire scar, it’s then more prone to burn again, creating a feedback loop of more fire and more cheatgrass. 

Alicia Hummel, a rangeland management specialist for the Bureau of Land Management’s Cody Field Office, addresses reporters inside the Red Canyon Fire scar in June 2026 (Hannah Nikonow/Intermountain West Joint Venture)

Those conditions are why Alicia Hummel called this spring’s persistent drought a “worst case scenario” for a landscape that’s still recovering from the Red Canyon Fire. Blueish perennial grasses that sprouted near the Bureau of Land Management rangeland manager’s feet were dominated by much-taller cheatgrass, an invasive annual grass that’s slowly overtaking Wyoming and the Bighorn Basin. 
“Those should be outgrowing the cheatgrass right now,” Hummel said. “It’s just so stunted. We shouldn’t have the cheatgrass exceeding our [native] perennials.” 
Native perennial grasses at only “a half or even a third” of their typical height and volume is a bad formula for the future of cheatgrass, which thrives in disturbed areas and especially burned landscapes. Native grasses can gain a toehold and help keep cheatgrass at bay, but that’s a less likely outcome when they’re being so clearly outcompeted. 
Intermountain West Joint Venture staffer Hannah Nikonow shows journalists year-old and fresh-grown cheatgrass in the Red Canyon Fire scar in June 2026. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
The federal wildfire and land managers were gathered alongside state, county and University of Wyoming officials to teach roughly a dozen journalists, most from out of state, about the elaborate process of restoring rangeland after wildfire in a landscape where invasive grasses are already widespread. The outing was organized by Intermountain West Joint Venture, a Missoula-based partnership group that focuses on “people-centric” approaches to conserving western habitat. 
More fire coming soon? 
As the caravan of reporters, land and weed managers and scientists toured the burned swath of Hot Springs County, state officials were gearing up for what’s expected to be a “tough year” for wildfire.
“If you look at the drought monitor, you will see dark red,” Gov. Mark Gordon said on May 28 at an annual interagency wildfire briefing. “[That] means there’s a fire danger that is far higher than it’s been in a long time.” 
Two weeks later, the entirety of Hot Springs County remains in “severe” drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Other areas in Wyoming have it worse: 15 of the state’s 23 counties included at least some areas where drought is considered “extreme.” Some blasts of spring snow and rainfall helped somewhat, but were not enough to pull areas out of drought, according to Wyoming State Forestry Division spokeswoman Melissa DeFrantis.
Hills on the right side of this gulch in the Bridger Mountains were not burned by the Red Canyon Fire. The slopes to the left lost their sagebrush overstory, which could take decades to grow back if it returns at all. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
And so the wildfire season has already arrived, even in the western mountains. When roughly 250 acres burned near Sagebrush Flat west of Togwotee Pass last month, the Bridger-Teton National Forest experienced its largest May wildfire in history. 
The grim outlook comes in the wake of two consecutive big Wyoming wildfire years. In 2024, the state confronted the second-most acres burned in its history, trailing only 1988. 
Wyoming officials are fighting back against a future of more wildfires and more cheatgrass. 
There was a bygone era when many Wyoming weed and pest districts threw in the towel and did nothing to interrupt the cheatgrass-wildfire cycle. 
“For a lot of years in this state, for a lot of the counties — especially more heavily infested counties — [cheatgrass] was not on our priority list at all,” said Lindsey Woodward, the weed and pest coordinator for the Wyoming Department of Agriculture. 
The mentality at the time, Woodward said, was: “We have no tools, we have no time, we have no budget, we’re not going to win — we’re just not going to [treat] it.” 
Fighting back
That attitude has abated. 
Nowadays, the Wyoming Weed and Pest Council facilitates massive efforts to address cheatgrass and other invasive annual grasses. 
“We have, in the last 10 or so years, really really pushed for bigger landscape-scale projects — watershed-sized projects,” Woodward said. 
During the last three legislative sessions, Wyoming lawmakers have fought over funding levels for spraying cheatgrass that enables those projects. Tens of millions of dollars have ultimately been made available after each fight. That’s helped, but experts say it’s still not enough to hold the line on invasive grasses that have already affected over a quarter of Wyoming’s landmass.
Partly that’s because of the exorbitant cost of spraying cheatgrass. 
The most effective herbicide, Rejuvra, provides enduring protection against cheatgrass, but spraying quickly runs up a steep bill. Woodward used the term “staggering” to describe the per-gallon cost. 
“It’s about $1,100 a gallon,” she said. 
Largely for that reason, Hot Springs County Weed and Pest District Supervisor Heather Love applied for $9.8 million to treat the Red Canyon Fire scar. 

The seed mix used to revegetate the Red Canyon Fire comes from Manderson-based Wind River Seed and includes a mix of bluebunch wheatgrass, Indian ricegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, western wheatgrass, Wyoming big sagebrush, saltbush and other native species. (Hannah Nikonow/Intermountain West Joint Venture)

Some spraying is already underway, though there could be years of effort ahead before the restoration work is complete, Woodward said. Spraying blackened ground can be counterproductive, because it can also kill native perennial grasses trying to reestablish. Reseeding can also delay spraying. 
“By the time you consider all of that … some of these projects are three or four years before you’ve completed the steps,” Woodward said. 
Ultimately, the costly and complex landscape recovery efforts will help ranchers whose cattle and sheep graze within the Red Canyon Fire scar.  
Out on the fire scar tour, the stewards of the V Ranch — where the blaze began — recounted confronting the wildfire and their experience helping the landscape heal in the 10 months that have since lapsed.
“Proper grazing is critical,” said Jim Wilson, whose granddaughter, Emme Norsworthy, will become the family’s fifth generation overseeing the ranch. 
Left to right, Billie Jo Norsworthy, Emme Norsworthy, and Jim and Terry Wilson recount the experience of watching and responding to the 2025 Red Canyon Fire burn over their V Ranch, a working cattle operation, in June 2026. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
“The BLM is right,” Wilson said about the need to rest rangelands from grazing after wildfires, motioning to his own federal allotment. “That country will probably not get grazed for two more years. We’re gonna let it grow up, let it go to seed.” 
Wilson was sanguine about Red Canyon Fire’s long-term impact on his ranch and adjoining allotments. The blaze could actually do some good for wildlife and cattle alike, he said. 
“All old sagebrush is not good,” Wilson said. “They’ve got to have new sagebrush, they’ve got to have forbs.”
But to ensure the land’s productivity, Wilson, weed and pest professionals, the BLM, and others will have to make sure that cheatgrass doesn’t take over. 
Ian Tator, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s statewide terrestrial habitat manager, spoke to how thresholds of invasive grass cover can make or break the habitat for mule deer. Cheatgrass coverage greater than 10% can cause the struggling ungulate species to avoid an area; 20% coverage can trigger habitat abandonment. 
“We want to work really hard to not let it get to that point,” Tator said.
The post Drought delivers ‘worst case scenario’ for fire scar recovery in Wyoming’s Bighorn Basin appeared first on WyoFile .

title: Exhibit features Casper artist’s ‘Late Nights and Long Summers’
description:
Zachary Pullen's nationally renowned illustrations portray the warmth and cheekiness of Americana and Wyoming life.
The post Exhibit features Casper artist’s ‘Late Nights and Long Summers’ appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Intrigued by all things Wyoming — its people, places and history — Casper illustrator Zachary Pullen has a knack for portraying the warmth and idiosyncrasies of America and the Cowboy State.
There’s a cheekiness to his work, he says, that comes from growing up on “Jaws,” “Caddyshack” and “Stand By Me.” 
The “Late Nights and Long Summers” exhibit at The Nicolaysen Art Museum in Casper includes Zachary Pullen’s preliminary and final sketches for his “Mick McMurry Code of Ethics” mural. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Though nationally renowned, Pullen describes himself as an average Wyoming working man who mostly lives on commissioned work, which he prefers to fulfill during the fall and winter months. That’s when he labors in his home studio for 17-hour stints that go well into the night.
“I work really late nights, from about October to May, and then I try to take the summers off and recharge for the next fall and winter,” Pullen told WyoFile.
Thus, the title of his latest exhibit, “Late Nights and Long Summers,” now showing at The Nicolaysen Art Museum in Casper. Pullen packed The Nic with some 200 works, including originals from his book collaborations: “A Home for Steamboat,” “The Rowdy Randy Wild West Show,” “The Christmas Ass” and “Among Giants.”
The “Late Nights and Long Summers” exhibit at The Nicolaysen Art Museum in Casper includes originals from Zachary Pullen’s collections “The Rowdy Randy Wild West Show” and “The Christmas Ass.” (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile) Credit: Dustin Bleizeffer
The exhibit drew hundreds of people during NIC Fest earlier this month — an opportunity for Pullen to mix with exhibitgoers eager to learn about the people (golfers, former Wyoming governors) and places (Devils Tower, Independence Rock, Hole-in-the-Wall) portrayed in his work.
Pullen, a bit of a history buff and a full-blown cultural observer, was more than happy to oblige. “Everybody wants to know something about something, which is really cool.”
“Late Nights and Long Summers” shows through August.

title: If you asked a park a question
description:
As America’s 250th nears, columnist Jessica Brauer takes to the field to find out what Wyoming's physical and abstract landscapes have to say about themselves.
The post If you asked a park a question appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Early in the warm season, while our neighbors fired up their fishing boats and pulled their camper trailers out for the summer’s first night under the stars, my little family wandered Curt Gowdy State Park with backpacks of field recorders, notebooks and cameras. Some folks glanced, questioning; others asked, “So, what are you doing here?” to which we said, “We’re interviewing the park.” 

Opinion

Can the lone pine at the treeline remember its years as a sapling?
How does the herd of antelope feel when the winter’s snow never comes?
Does a mountain know it will one day erode to just a hill?
We came to the southern Wyoming park, situated between Laramie and Cheyenne, through the Wyoming Arts Council and Wyoming State Parks’ 2026 Artist in Residence Program, which was expanded this year with semiquincentennial funding. Through the summer and fall, 19 Wyoming artists will take up four-day residencies in parks across the state — each asked to honor the past, reflect on the present and imagine the future of America as it celebrates 250 years. 
Field recorders, notebooks and cameras filled backpacks on an excursion to interview Curt Gowdy State Park. (Jessica Brauer)
We pitched our project as an exploration of landscape, both physical and abstract. We were curious what Wyoming chooses to say about itself through the care of and connection to its parks. What better time to listen to the wisdom of the land and its creatures, when communication between humans feels so fraught. 
Established in 1971 through a lease agreement with the city of Cheyenne and the Boy Scouts, the area was originally named Granite State Park. Today, it’s known for miles of hiking and mountain biking trails, camping, fishing and water recreation in Granite, Crystal and North Crow reservoirs. 

Eyes shut, tongue out, Jo the pup takes it all in. (Jessica Brauer)

Long before our founding fathers declared this America, wisdom lived in places like this. It was surely known intimately for food, medicine and ceremony — a far richer relationship than the one forged with 30-foot camper trailers and speed boats blasting pop country. 
One year after the park’s creation, Wyoming renamed it after beloved national sports broadcaster and Wyoming native Curt Gowdy. 
Gowdy knew of the land’s wisdom, too. In “Cowboy at the Mike,” his autobiography co-written with Al Hirshberg, he wrote: “Everybody dressed the same for fishing — in boots and Levi’s — so you never knew if you were with a millionaire rancher or one of his hired hands. You didn’t care either.”
Three nights in the mountains was far too short a time to solve the challenges that face America’s future, but, as with most any time when phones sit untouched, it was nourishing. We remembered to pay closer attention to our company.
We talked of how the wind wonders why we grip our belongings so tightly and how the reservoir of drinking water watches us paddle with our fluorescent, fiberglass fins. We questioned whether a root-bound tree felt relief when it finally fell onto the shore, and why people insist on carving their initials into everything.
Does a root-bound tree finally feel relief once it falls onto the shore? (Jessica Brauer)
What did the park say about America?
Well, nothing. 
Though there was no shortage of depictions of the stars and stripes stretched high on camper awnings and low, printed across swim trunks. When we visited the roadside bar for a burger and a hot-water handwash, the house band called the room to stand and sing along to the national anthem. Meanwhile, the park sat down the highway, waiting with its quiet. 
Instead, it said our shadows all look the same in the midday sun, and the ripples on the lake are only the first layer of many. That we try to explain away the truth with time, and so much has remained unchanged.
Perhaps for its birthday, America should spend a week outdoors.

title: Alabama medical cannabis dispensary sees over 100 patients in first week
description: Over 100 qualifying patients have purchased medical cannabis since Alabama’s first dispensary opened, the Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission said Thursday. The state’s first legal medical cannabis provider, Callie’s Apothecary, opened its first location in Montgomery on June 4 following a “soft opening” the day before. Justin Aday, general counsel for the c[...]
text:
Mock medical cannabis lozenges in a display case at Callie's Apothecary in Montgomery, Alabama, on May 14, 2026. The dispensary, Alabama's first, has seen over 100 patients since it opened on June 4. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Over 100 qualifying patients have purchased medical cannabis since Alabama’s first dispensary opened, the Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission said Thursday.
The state’s first legal medical cannabis provider, Callie’s Apothecary, opened its first location in Montgomery on June 4 following a “soft opening” the day before. Justin Aday, general counsel for the commission, said Thursday that 102 patients have purchased medical cannabis products in 111 transactions. Those transactions have generated about $14,600 in pre-tax sales with the average transaction being $131.56, Aday said.
Vince Schilleci, owner of Callie’s, said in a phone interview Thursday afternoon that the last week of business has been rewarding.
“I’m seeing a lot of happy patients,” he said. “Our store manager saw a patient walking out, and as silly as it sounds, they jumped and clicked their heels. Yeah, they were that happy about having that medicine.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the patient menu on Callie’s website, each product ranges from $42 to $52 each. Schilleci said that the dispensary got its second shipment of products on Thursday and expects another one on Friday, which will help meet the demand of patients.
“We’ve had to – I hate to use this term ration –  but we’ve limited how much patients could purchase, just because we knew how many patients were coming on board, and we at least wanted people to have a chance to have something,” Schilleci said. “We’ve lifted the rationing now, so patients can come down and buy their full 60-day allotment if they choose.”
Aday said that as of Thursday morning, 481 patients have applied for a cannabis card and 446 of them have been issued one by the AMCC. 
The Alabama medical cannabis law, enacted in 2021, allows registered physicians to recommend cannabis for about 15 medical conditions, including cancer, depression, Parkinson’s Disease, PTSD, sickle-cell anemia, chronic pain, and terminal diseases. The approved product forms are restricted to tablets, tinctures, patches, oils, and gel cubes (only peach flavor), with raw plant material and smokable forms remaining prohibited.
As of Thursday, there are 52 physicians certified to recommend medical cannabis to patients in Alabama, according to the Alabama Board of Medical Examiners. Aday said 39 are registered with the AMCC, with three pending, and 21 of the physicians have made medical cannabis recommendations to patients.


Dispensary Locations:
CCS of Alabama, LLC

Montgomery, Bessemer and Talladega

GP6 Wellness, LLC

Birmingham, Athens and Attalla

RJK Holdings, LLC

Oxford, Daphne and Mobile

Yellowhammer Medical Dispensary, LLC *pending license approval

Birmingham, Owens Cross Roads and Demopolis



“We’re certainly looking forward to more of these patients being able to get to that dispensary and seeing other dispensaries open that will provide more geographic coverage for them,” Aday said. “We’re working diligently with processors in the lab on new products that are being manufactured so that the dispensary can maintain an inventory of products and a variety of products in that inventory to serve the patients that are visiting them.”
Litigation has also held up access to medical cannabis. Some firms sued the commission for not being awarded a license, citing a discriminatory process. Another case involved five parents that sued the commission over delays in access to cannabis, which was dismissed in August. 
Licenses for three of the four possible dispensary companies were not approved until December.
Three of the companies, CCS of Alabama, LLC, GP6 Wellness, LLC, and RJK Holdings, LLC, have licenses and are expected to open their storefronts this summer, according to AMCC Director John McMillan. A fourth license is pending litigation, but is likely to go to Yellowhammer Medical Dispensaries, LLC.
“I would do it again just to see the smile on these patients’ faces. Now, I would hope a little bit easier, but it’s been worth it,” Schilleci said. “It’s been worth it. There’s no doubt.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee waste task force eyes changes to law allowing local rejection of landfills
description: Tennessee lawmakers and other members of the state’s Solid Waste Task Force hinted Tuesday that they are considering changing a law that has allowed local governing bodies to approve or deny landfill proposals for nearly 40 years. The idea of slimming down local control over the landfill permitting process has support from business interest groups […]
text:
As Tennessee landfills, like the one pictured here, fill up, state lawmakers are considering dialing back a law giving local boards control over the permitting of new ones. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee lawmakers and other members of the state’s Solid Waste Task Force hinted Tuesday that they are considering changing a law that has allowed local governing bodies to approve or deny landfill proposals for nearly 40 years.
The idea of slimming down local control over the landfill permitting process has support from business interest groups who describe the state’s layers of local approval as a “bottleneck” preventing new landfill sites from getting the green light as existing landfills creep closer to maximum capacity.
The problem, they say, is that too many communities are using powers afforded by state laws to block plans for new or expanded landfills.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“It’s really easy to say no to everything, but you still have a problem that you have to deal with, and I believe we’re seeing a lot of that when people say, ‘well, we don’t want it … but we’re not willing to deal with what we have’ … it really gets under my skin,” said Rep. Rusty Grills, a Newbern Republican.
Counties and cities have relied on a statute called the Jackson Law, which allows local government bodies that adopt the law with a two-thirds vote to ensure that no new landfill construction can begin without local approval. As of January, 54 counties and 18 cities have adopted the Jackson Law.
Regional waste boards that have submitted solid waste plans to the state may also vote on whether or not a landfill proposal fits within those plans. Separately, a provision added to the Scenic Rivers Act in 1990 insulates certain rivers from landfill operations within two miles on either side.
These factors are at the center of multiple legal battles. After the Marshall/Maury Municipal Solid Waste Planning Region Board halted the installation of landfills on land previously owned by the Monsanto Chemical Company near the Duck River in 2023, the landowner filed two lawsuits challenging the board’s decision and the use of the Scenic Rivers Act, zoning and the Jackson Law to prevent the landfill from moving forward — something they say renders their land valueless. The lawsuits are ongoing.
Opposition to landfills is increasingly in the spotlight as permits for new and expanded landfills are rejected at the local level. (Photo: Jesi Mink)
Compliance with zoning ordinances, approval from regional waste boards and approval from governing bodies in localities that have adopted the Jackson Law are needed for a permit to move on from the first step of the state’s permitting process, said Nickolaus Lytle, the solid waste permits manager for the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation, or TDEC. The entire permitting process can take between five and ten years, if not longer.
Industry operators would like to see Tennessee’s process become more regional, reducing layers of local approval, representatives for the National Waste and Recycling Association, or NWRA, said. RJ Gibson, director of government affairs for the Tennessee Chamber of Commerce, stopped short of recommending “abolishing the Jackson Law or removing local control.”
“We absolutely have to have a partnership with local governments in order to build these facilities, but the reality is … right now it is almost impossible,” Gibson said. “It’s very, very difficult to bring new capacity online … as a matter of math and economics, we’re going to need more solid waste capacity in the state, we just are. And so we have to … have a system that allows us to add that capacity.”
Lytle said his office processes about eight landfill expansions each year that require a full permit. He told the Solid Waste Task Force on Tuesday that recently, he’s seen more legal challenges over permits.
But residents in areas that have opposed new or growing landfills argued that local authority acts as an important stopgap, giving a say to the communities that must literally live alongside the results of landfill site decisions.
Michelle Trieschmann, a Scott County resident, business owner and vocal opponent of a proposed landfill near Oneida, said rural communities are “often at a disadvantage in these debates.”
While companies may have resources to hire lobbyists, attorneys, engineers and public relations firms, she said, local residents do not.
“Most of the time, all we get is a couple of minutes at a microphone to speak for our community,” Trieschmann told the task force during her allotted 3-minute comment period. This is why laws protecting local authority matter, she said.
Final version of scenic river protection bill scraps exemption for current landfill permits

“These laws … do not prevent responsible waste management,” she said. “What they do is help restore balance to a process where the people with the greatest stake in the outcome often have the fewest resources to influence it.”
Attorney: Degree of local control is ‘a policy question’
State legislators passed the Jackson Law, named for former lawmaker Doug Jackson of Dickson, in response to a commercial landfill boom in the 1980s. The law was initially intended to expire in 1991, but later amended to last indefinitely. Another amendment in 2013 grants local governing bodies that adopt the law approval authority over landfills seeking to change their classification to accept different types of waste.
The Jackson Law requires local governing bodies to evaluate landfill proposals based on type of waste, method of disposal, projected impact on surrounding property values, adequacy of existing infrastructure to handle increased traffic, economic impact, compatibility with existing zoning plans and “any other factor which may affect the public health, safety or welfare.”
Mallorie Kerby, a lobbyist representing the National Waste and Recycling Association’s Tennessee chapter, said these criteria are too broad and subjective.
Rep. Chris Todd, a Jackson Republican and co-chair of the Solid Waste Task Force, pointed to a Tennessee Attorney General opinion issued in 1998 stating that the law’s purpose was “to provide ‘local governments that do not have zoning ordinances’ the authority to review and approve … proposals for landfills and other solid waste facilities.”
Todd asked if the state has considered that the Jackson Law “should really only apply to local governments that do not have zoning.”
Deputy General Counsel Stephanie Durman cautioned against inferring the law’s intent, noting that the law itself does not say that.
Rep. Chris Todd, a Jackson Republican and co-chair of Tennessee’s Solid Waste Task Force. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“The question of whether the Jackson Law and local zoning should be dual levels of review is really a policy question for those of you who’ve actually been elected to office,” Durman said.
Former Tennessee Rep. Donna Barrett said seven other states have some version of the Jackson Law, though Tennessee’s is the strongest. Barrett lives in Rutherford County, home to the Middle Point Landfill that serves 27 other counties and six other states.
“We have a state law that the counties are responsible for their disposal, but yet we don’t require it to be in their county … this Jackson Law is a safeguard to say, not everybody’s trash in my backyard,” she said. “Until we make it more of a requirement that the counties … take care of their garbage instead of passing it on to somebody else, this Jackson Law is that stopgap.”
Jennifer Shockley, a Scott County resident, said 49 of Tennessee’s 95 counties do not have county-wide zoning codes.
“When we’re having a discussion about eliminating local control, those are the counties that you’re really going to be affecting,” she said.
Regionalization
Tennessee law also allows for regional planning boards, which are required to develop a long-term plan for waste in that region. Board members are appointed by county and city mayors in the region, with at least one member from each county.
Currently, eight multi-county boards (spanning 34 counties total) exist in the state, alongside 61 counties that operate single-county boards.
The boards are required to submit annual progress reports to the state, and a 2021 law clarified the regional review process for new landfills and expansions to require public hearings and written findings from the board, limiting denials to proposals that are inconsistent with the approved regional waste plan.
The NWRA wants those plans to be better vetted at the state level for feasibility and to “make sure from a state perspective that they fit together,” NWRA Vice President of Chapter Relations Katie Evans said. “If the plans are not quality plans, then that system is not functioning.”
Anna Rose Murphy and Joyce Keeton console each other after a bill to prevent a landfill from being sited near Big South Fork River in Scott County failed to pass. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
In other states, state environmental protection agencies typically have a larger role in determining whether landfills are needed, NWRA lobbyists said.
A recently passed law established a state policy to “ensure there’s enough landfill capacity for waste that cannot be recycled or recovered,” and allows TDEC to create rules and approve or disapprove regional plans based on whether they mesh with the state’s waste plan. Lobbyists called this a step in the right direction.
Ralph Trieschmann, a member of the Scott County Chamber of Commerce, discouraged the over-regionalization of these boards, emphasizing the importance of local knowledge. He pointed to Tennessee’s recent congressional redistricting, which placed rural Scott County in East Tennessee in the 6th district along with parts of Nashville.
“If the recent redistricting is any indication of how organizations are made out of our counties (for) our representation … I don’t know that we want to have that same kind of imposed regionalization on our waste management,” he said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Tennessee keeping intensive probation program alive – barely
description: The Tennessee Department of Correction is proposing a two-year contract to maintain the state’s Community Corrections program but keeping a 15% funding reduction in place, finagling with the funds in a mild case of Tin Man’s disease. The intensive probation program with 300 positions in 13 agencies across the state resurfaced a couple of years […]
text:
Limping along: The state's Community Corrections program, an intensive parole program, has garnered funds to remain operational for two years. (Photo: Brad Freeman, Metropolitan Nashville General Sessions Court)The Tennessee Department of Correction is proposing a two-year contract to maintain the state’s Community Corrections program but keeping a 15% funding reduction in place, finagling with the funds in a mild case of Tin Man’s disease.
The intensive probation program with 300 positions in 13 agencies across the state resurfaced a couple of years ago, after the state shut it down, but is treading water.
Senators asked TDOC to release money from a $14 million fund balance last year to keep Community Corrections agencies from shedding workers and losing day reporting centers for clients. Instead of using that fund to shore up Community Corrections, which was enacted by the legislature in 1985 as a last-ditch effort to keep people out of prison, the department used the entire balance to fund the program next fiscal year, starting in July, and labeled it as “non-recurring,” meaning there’s no guarantee it will be funded again.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
State budget officials testified that the program would be returned to the annual budget next year.
This sort of instability, though, puts Community Corrections agencies in limbo, making it difficult to hire workers, give an occasional bonus and guarantee they’ll have an office.
State Sen. Ed Jackson of Jackson has been lobbying hard – to no avail – with Gov. Bill Lee’s administration to find money to prop up the agencies, including one in Decatur County that had to close day reporting centers. He said he’s not giving up.
“That’s something I know we need to keep around,” Jackson told the Lookout this week. 
But while the state put money in the budget for the program this year and appears ready to offer two-year contracts, Jackson said the agencies “need to be made whole.” 
Jackson called the agencies “very effective” in keeping offenders out of prison. Graduates have told the Lookout that Community Corrections saved their lives, forcing them to kick addictions and get to work.
Yet it has been fighting to survive under Lee.
Davidson County Community Corrections keeps clients alive

The legislature ordered the governor’s administration to keep it going, but the Correction Department in 2023 under interim Commissioner Lisa Helton wrote a bid document requiring the agencies to become clinics with licensed counselors with master’s degrees, pretty much putting them out of business. 
The idea was to steer probation services to the Department of Correction, despite criticism that it doesn’t have enough officers to serve people already incarcerated. Organizations such as Men of Valor, a faith-based prison ministry supported by Lee, have found more favor, even though they’re not set by state law. 
Correction Commissioner Frank Strada has kept it limping along, refusing to use the fund balance to bolster program agencies last year when he said the department wants “transparent stewardship” of the funds, which are tied to Community Corrections but “must be aligned with budgetary guidelines, operational planning and the broader strategic priorities of the state.”
Thank you for the word salad. 
Judges accustomed to sentencing offenders to Community Corrections raised enough ruckus to force the program’s revival. But it quickly became so popular that when agencies reopened, there wasn’t enough money to fully fund them, putting them in dire straits.
Jackson said he’s been “preaching from the rooftop” but hasn’t gotten the right people to listen.
He’s hoping a new governor and, potentially, a new correction commissioner will take a different view.
Predicting a state win
Lt. Gov. Randy McNally said Thursday he is “disappointed” that Metro Nashville filed suit against the state to stop it from taking over appointments to five airport boards.
McNally said the state contributes more money to the airport than Metro Nashville and added, “I think that the law we have will survive any challenge.”
Metro Nashville won a previous lawsuit over the state’s effort to control the airport authority, based on Tennessee’s Home Rule Amendment, which prohibits the state from singling out city and county governments without their approval.
Metro sues state again to block airport board takeover

This time, Metro Nashville is arguing that a 2024 Federal Aviation Administration Reauthorization Act allows local governments to refuse to acquiesce to the state in airport board takeovers.
“That law was designed precisely for this situation,” Metro Law Director Wally Dietz told the Metro Nashville Airport Authority Wednesday.
Metro Nashville officials want to protect their ability to control the property at and around the airport, and they also think the state’s move violates federal law.
Some airport board members seemed agitated that Metro would not be paying its legal fees as Dietz proposed the hiring of an outside legal team. He pointed out that Metro legal had done 90% of the work preparing to file the suit.
After going into executive session out of the public view, the board opted to limit legal expenses to $100,000.
Airport Authority President and CEO Doug Kreulen also expressed concerns about getting tied up in the legal battle between Metro and the state, saying airlines don’t want the airport to get “bogged down” in a long legal fight and potentially pass costs on to customers, who don’t care about much except on-time flights and luggage.
No doubt, he is correct. But airplanes don’t fly within a vacuum. 
Keeping kids off floors
The State Building Commission moved forward Thursday with plans for the Department of Children’s Services to build three facilities, totaling $30 million, to take children into state custody.
About 350 children a month entered DCS custody in 2026, and the state has nearly 8,370 youths in its care.
Constructing places to take them in and provide temporary housing and care is a novel approach, considering some of these abused and neglected children have been sleeping on office floors at various times over the last five to six years.  
Margie Quin, commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Children’s Services, photographed at the Cordell Hull Legislative Office Building, says the problem of having kids in state custody sleeping on the floors of office buildings has been solved. (John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
DCS Commissioner Margie Quin told the Lookout Thursday that no children have been staying overnight in state offices since January. Instead, they’ve been placed in transitional homes or moved into foster care, kinfolks or residential treatment, according to the department.
There’s nothing like moving at the speed of light. The Lookout first covered this problem in 2021. 
But better late than never.
The state will construct the first three of these buildings in Jonesborough, Tullahoma and Lexington, Quin said. Several more are planned, and DCS is looking at sites in Nashville and northeast Tennessee.
In addition, the state will start contracting with pediatricians and dentists to provide services to children when they enter state custody at the new locations, enabling DCS to resolve audit findings by the Tennessee Comptroller’s Office.
Welcome to Tennessee, now get the …
Lee once said he wakes up every morning thinking about tourism. While that might seem a little weird, he backed that up with a $5 million campaign to promote scenic beauty and welcome folks to Tennessee, including new signs at the state lines.
The signs have the State Capitol sitting in the midst of hills, mountains and rivers. Someone mentioned it’s a tip of the cap to Tennessee’s rural lawmakers, most of whom hate its biggest cities but love to party in downtown Nashville.
To be sure, they’re not as mundane as the old ones. But the question is: Does anyone care about road signs? The fewer the better, unless you’ve got to go to the john.
And do we really need to spend millions of dollars promoting a state that needs no promotion when kids have been sleeping on office floors, probation programs have been laying off people and immigrant kids are going to be reported to Immigration and Customs Enforcement instead of receiving healthcare treatment?
New signs welcoming visitors to Tennessee are soon to be hosted at 16 interstate entry points. (Photo: Tn.gov)
Speaking of money
Lee is the fifth-highest paid governor in the country, making nearly $240,000 a year. He comes in behind the governor of Pennsylvania at $253,870 and the head honchos of New York, California and Massachusetts, according to a Tennessean report.
McNally defended Lee, saying he’s been “extremely valuable” to the state. He said states such as California, which has a budget deficit, and New York are struggling financially. Tennessee is required by law to balance its budget.
Lee, who distanced himself from Lee Co. — the HVAC company founded by his grandfather — but loaned his campaign nearly $5.6 million in 2018, is taking his salary while former Govs. Bill Haslam and Phil Bredesen gave theirs back to the state. 
“Yeah, it was hard to give up / Some things are hard to let go / Some things are never enough” *
* Tom Petty, “Love Is a Long Road”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Corruption scandals from Denver to Washington dragged down Republicans as the 1876 election began
description: Despite the pomp and circumstance of the Centennial, the summer of 1876 was a fraught and anxious period for the Republican Party.
text:
An 1876 illustration shows the nomination of Rutherford B. Hayes at the Republican National Convention in Cincinnati. Anxieties over Republicans' electoral fortunes and the future of Reconstruction were a major factor shaping party politics in the Colorado Territory. (Library of Congress)Territorial Gov. John Routt, former congressional delegate Jerome Chaffee and Central City attorney Henry Teller were among the dignitaries who traveled in early June 1876 from the Colorado Territory to Cincinnati, where the Republican National Convention gaveled in at the city’s Exposition Hall.



← June 4–10
June 11–17 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

Despite the upcoming 100th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence and the pomp and circumstance of the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, the summer of 1876 was a fraught and anxious period for the Republican Party.
Two years earlier, Democrats had won control of the House of Representatives for the first time since the Civil War. With much of the country still reeling from the economic effects of the Panic of 1873, the opposition party now hoped to follow it up with victory in the 1876 presidential election — a grim prospect for Republicans and northerners to whom the Democratic Party still stood as a symbol of rebellion and Confederacy. The fate of Reconstruction, under which the federal government had acted to secure Black civil rights in the South, hung in the balance.
Colorado’s admission to the union in the Centennial year was little more than a partisan political maneuver by Republicans, who felt assured of the new state’s three electoral votes. In early 1875, the lame-duck GOP Congress had passed a Colorado statehood act even as it defeated a similar measure for Democratic-leaning New Mexico, which wouldn’t be admitted as a state until 1912.
Up until early 1876, President Ulysses S. Grant had given serious consideration to running for an unprecedented third term. But he eventually bowed out as his administration continued to be rocked by one corruption scandal after another, including the Whiskey Ring bribery scheme and similar allegations that led to the resignations of two Cabinet secretaries and the impeachment of another.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Chaffee and Teller were bitter political rivals but had been two of the six delegates to the RNC elected at a territorial GOP convention held in April — and before the year was over, they would both be elected by the inaugural Colorado General Assembly as the Centennial State’s first two U.S. senators.
It was an awkward time to be a member of the Colorado Territory’s fledgling Republican political establishment: Climbing the ranks meant currying favor with party bosses who controlled coveted appointments to territorial offices and civil service positions, but doing so carried the risk of being tainted by the aura of corruption and scandal that plagued Grant’s administration in his second term.
In the early 1870s, Chaffee and Teller led different factions within the party that traded charges of graft and carpetbagging as they battled to install their favored candidates as governor, postmaster, U.S. marshal, surveyor general and other posts, subject to presidential and congressional approval. The departure of Teller-backed Gov. Edward McCook in 1875, to be replaced by Routt, had been a victory for Chaffee and the “Denver Ring,” who found themselves ascendant once again in the party’s territorial affairs.
Jerome B. Chaffee was elected one of Colorado’s first two U.S. senators in 1876. (Library of Congress)
Even as Colorado Republicans traveled to Cincinnati to select a new presidential nominee, former U.S. Marshal Mark Shaffenburg remained on trial in Denver, having been indicted for embezzling government funds by overcharging for prisoner expenses and mileage. Shaffenburg also stood accused of aiding a fraudulent land-grab scheme in southern Colorado, a scheme that also ensnared railroad baron David Moffat and other members of the Denver Ring.
On June 14 — the same day the GOP convention opened — the jury in Shaffenburg’s case told a federal judge in Denver that it could not reach a verdict “after nearly ninety hours of enforced retirement and alleged ‘deliberation,’” the Rocky Mountain News reported. Indictments against Moffat and other alleged perpetrators of the land-grab scheme were later dropped.
GOP convention
Among the resolutions adopted into the territorial party’s platform in April 1876 was one professing “unshaken … faith in the principles and policy of the Republican Party” while stating “a disposition to reform the civil service of the country, and to exact from officials charged with the administration of public affairs a rigid honesty and a scrupulous observance of their obligations.”
James Belford, another RNC delegate elected by the Colorado convention, delivered a “ringing speech” to the party faithful gathered at the Denver Theater, the Rocky Mountain News reported.
“He deplored the spots on the face of the Republican sun, but said the party was purging itself of scoundrels,” wrote the News. “The delegates just elected would, in convention at Cincinnati, support the man in favor of reform in the civil service and the development of the mineral resources of the country, the basis of national wealth.”
Meeting for their convention in the crucial swing state of Ohio, Republicans deadlocked on the first six ballots as the favorite for nomination, former House Speaker James G. Blaine of Maine, failed to capture a majority. On the seventh, they instead nominated Ohio Gov. Rutherford B. Hayes, a dark-horse candidate untainted by the reputation for corruption that threatened to sink the GOP’s electoral chances.
The Rocky Mountain News, ever the loyal mouthpiece of Denver Republicans, rushed to applaud the selection of the man it branded “Honest Hayes.”
“Not a man in public life possesses a purer record and clearer character than Gov. Hayes,” the News claimed. “A representative Republican, he also satisfies all the requirements of the reform sentiment now so popular, never having affiliated in the least degree with any of the baser elements of the party.”
The paper also couldn’t help but boast about its own prediction, at the outset of the convention, that Blaine was a weaker candidate than he appeared, and that he would win by the second ballot or not at all.
“Those who thought The News went off wrong, to use a comprehensive conversationalism, when it discounted the chances of Blaine for the nomination of the Cincinnati convention,” wrote the paper’s editors, “have got something to put in their pipes and smoke this morning.”



Selected sources

The Rocky Mountain News, June 15–17, 1876
West, Elliott. “Jerome B. Chaffee and the McCook-Elbert Fight,” Colorado Magazine, Spring 1969

title: Prevailing PSC candidates say campaign work not done with Dem opponents on horizon
description: The candidates who vied for a pair of seats on the commission that regulates utilities in North Dakota have vowed to continue their work, but in different ways.  The two Republican incumbents on the Public Service Commission, Sheri Haugen-Hoffart and Jill Kringstad, won their primary contests with 64% and 54% of the vote respectively. They […]
text:
Public Service Commissioners Sheri Haugen-Hoffart, left and Jill Kringstad (Photos courtesy of PSC).The candidates who vied for a pair of seats on the commission that regulates utilities in North Dakota have vowed to continue their work, but in different ways. 
The two Republican incumbents on the Public Service Commission, Sheri Haugen-Hoffart and Jill Kringstad, won their primary contests with 64% and 54% of the vote respectively. They defeated Deven Styczynski, who was endorsed by the GOP at the party’s state convention, and Chris Olson. 
Haugen-Hoffart and Kringstad acknowledged the job isn’t done. Both face Democratic opponents in the general election. More than 26,000 voters supported Styczynski and around 35,000 cast ballots for Olson. Both incumbents received significantly fewer votes than Rep. Julie Fedorchak who was at the top of the Republican ticket. 
“We’re all under the same party, the Republican Party, and you’ll see me out there across this whole great state working hard and listening to the voters and gaining their trust,” Haugen-Hoffart said.
North Dakota Public Service Commission incumbents defeat Republican challengers

It was the first time Kringstad’s name appeared on the ballot. Gov. Kelly Armstrong appointed her to the commission in 2025. She said she can’t speak to the motivations of the voters who supported her opponent, but will continue introducing herself to the public ahead of November. 
“I’m just going to continue to talk about the message that I think is important to North Dakotans, which is how we’re going to continue to have the lowest electric rates in the nation, while at the same time balancing development with landowner rights,” Kringstad said.
Styczynski said the public service commissioners’ electoral underperformance compared to Fedorchak shows voters have real concerns about electricity rates, data center development and industrial projects “that just are showing up out of nowhere.”
“Money won the election. That’s how I look at it,” Styczynski said. “The work isn’t over. Just because you lose an election doesn’t mean there isn’t stuff to do.”
 
More primary 2026 coverage


Styczynski said his loss to Haugen-Hoffart will not stop him from continuing to fight for the policy priorities he advocated on the campaign trail. Although not a lawmaker, he is drafting legislation to restore local control over energy project permitting and to require environmental impact assessments for large energy consumers like data centers. 
He hopes to recruit legislators to sponsor the bills in the 2027 legislative session.
Haugen-Hoffart will face Democratic nominee John Pederson, a professor at Mayville State University, in the general election.
Kringstad will face off against Scot Kelsh, a former Fargo firefighter and Democratic state lawmaker, for the two-year term in the general election. 
Olson did not return a phone call and text message seeking comment for this article.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: 30,000 Idahoans had to drop health insurance from the state exchange this year. Why don’t we care?
description: We’re making America “great” again, and I hope you are embracing these changes. I’ll skip over the deportations and go straight to healthcare, since that is, I believe, the weakness that will bring this nation to its knees. Most other countries have looked at this problem, had some hard discussions, and solved it. Most who […]
text:
America is the richest country in the world right now. And we are pushing millions onto the healthcare cliff, writes guest columnist Dan Schmidt. (Photo by Getty Images)We’re making America “great” again, and I hope you are embracing these changes. I’ll skip over the deportations and go straight to healthcare, since that is, I believe, the weakness that will bring this nation to its knees.
Most other countries have looked at this problem, had some hard discussions, and solved it. Most who have are just as “free,” “democratic,” and “first world” as us. America is the richest country in the world right now. And we are pushing millions onto the healthcare cliff. 
One false step, one bad disease, and you are bankrupt. How does this make us Great Again?
After health insurance subsidies end, 30,000 Idahoans will be uninsured, government report says

Let’s just look at Idaho; forget the national picture.
About 30,000 Idahoans have decided to go bare. That’s the number of folks who have dropped out of the state health insurance exchange this year. They are willing to stand on the cliff without a rope. 
Let’s back up. 
The state exchange was created as part of the Affordable Care Act = ACA = Obamacare to get people affordable health insurance when they made more money than would allow them to qualify for Medicaid, which is health insurance for the REALLY poor. On the exchange, Idahoans could get federal income tax credits to help pay for their health insurance. 
But MAGA cut that.
We’re not talking about Medicaid here. We’re talking about low-middle income folks — working, maybe self-employed, small business folks — who have decided they can’t afford health insurance. 
Is this making us GREAT? Again?
The insurance companies understand the market. They know there will be billions of unpaid care given when the folks who chose to go bare fall off the cliff and are wheeled in. And the hospitals will shift the costs to those who do pay: the insured. So they have raised their rates.
Can you see the connection? Most other countries see it. Why don’t we? 
If we have everybody in the pool, we all have to pay less. And we all receive the safety rope. And we aren’t out on the edge of the cliff.
Medicaid is down there at the bottom, the very poor. Idaho is working as hard as it can to get as many of those “losers” kicked off coverage. Maybe you don’t think they are worthy. Then just go ahead and say it. The insurance companies, the small-town hospitals, they see this coming.
Just one premature baby, one fall off a ladder and you lose your house — everything.
Small aside here: Under the Medicaid “work requirements” bill passed by the Idaho Legislature, most legislators would not qualify for Medicaid, let alone the gold-plated health insurance us taxpayers pay for their benefit.
Idaho Legislature passes bill for Medicaid expansion work requirements by 2027

The “good” old days, back when America was GREAT, people got sick. Maybe they got care, maybe they didn’t. According to our state attorney general, nobody died because they couldn’t access health care. Maybe you share his view.
But I could tell you stories. How I cared for the uninsured. How I worked to make sure they got care. But then, did the hospital come after them? Did the medical claims attorneys file their claims? Did they lose their tools, their homes? Saving a life and destroying a livelihood. GREAT AGAIN?
Does this make any sense to you?
How can we be the richest country in the world and we aren’t willing to sit down and discuss this immense problem?
Idahoans will suffer. Just a couple or a dozen or a hundred of those 30,000 without health insurance might slip off the precipice. They may die. That would be cheap. 
Shouldn’t we be all in this for them to live and recover to the best state of health that they can?
Maybe you don’t think so. Maybe you think we should all be in this for ourselves. Our attorney general thinks so. Do you?
I can tell you, our North Idaho Congressman Russ Fulcher would not be alive if he didn’t have good taxpayer funded health insurance. But he works diligently to make sure less of us have such access. The hypocrisy.
Maybe that’s what we’ve come to. Just take what you can, and the rest of us be damned. Great Again.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Wes Allen, John Wahl face each other in GOP runoff for lt. governor
description: Republican voters on Tuesday will choose between two social conservatives as their nominee for lieutenant governor.  The runoff will feature John Wahl, the former chair of the Alabama Republican Party, who received 192,432 votes (40.56%) in the May 19 primary, and Alabama Secretary of State Wes Allen, who received 180,292 votes (38%). The winner of […]
text:
Alabama Secretary of State Wes Allen (left) will face former Alabama Republican Party Chairman John Wahl in a runoff for lieutenant governor. (Photo of Allen courtesy of candidate, Wes Allen by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector; Graphic by Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Republican voters on Tuesday will choose between two social conservatives as their nominee for lieutenant governor. 
The runoff will feature John Wahl, the former chair of the Alabama Republican Party, who received 192,432 votes (40.56%) in the May 19 primary, and Alabama Secretary of State Wes Allen, who received 180,292 votes (38%).
The winner of the runoff will face Democratic nominee Phillip Ensler, a state representative from Montgomery, in the fall election.
The job of lieutenant governor is effectively powerless. While the office once had influence over the Senate comparable to that of the House Speaker, with the lieutenant governor appointing committees and controlling the flow of legislation, those powers were transferred to the Senate President Pro Tem in 1999 after a lengthy stand-off between then-Lt. Gov. Steve Windom, a Republican, and what was then the Democratic-controlled Senate. 
The Senate this spring further reduced the lieutenant governor’s appointment powers. The occupant of the chair presides over the Senate and becomes governor should that office become vacant.
However, candidates for the position have said they will try to wield the office to advance goals.
“I want to bring in people that are already in government to get around the table and make sure that we identify any potential fraud, identify any potential waste and identify any potential abuse that’s going on within state government,” Allen said in an interview on Wednesday. “It would be naive of us to look at what was going on in the federal government when President Trump came in his second term and set up the DOGE actions, to think that is not happening in some type of form in Alabama state government.”
Wahl said in an interview Wednesday evening that the position has more power than people think.
“It is the second highest position in the state. It comes with a bully pulpit, but more importantly, it’s kind of the bridge between the executive branch and the legislative branch, and I think that’s important to remember because that comes with the ability to affect policy and at the end of the day that’s what a good leader does, they try to affect policy for the people of the state,” he said.
Wahl has previously led efforts to restrict content in his position as chairman of the Alabama Public Library Service which most recently voted to withhold funding for Fairhope Public Library, claiming books shelved by the library contained sexually explicit material. Library officials have said the definitions are not clear and Fairhope has refused to reshelve the books. 
To ensure his priorities are addressed, Allen said he’d use his relationships within the Senate and his previous political experience.
“Because of my experience in the judicial branch, because of my experience in the legislative branch, because of my experience now in the executive branch, bringing all of that to bear, and those relationships in that Alabama State Senate I can go to the (President) Pro Tem (Garlan) Gudger (R-Cullman), I can go to a particular senator and say, ‘Hey, I just heard this from somebody, what’s your thoughts on this? This is something we may need to look into,’”
During his campaign, Allen engaged with anti-Muslim rhetoric, stating in a Facebook post in March that he would never enter a mosque or Islamic Center. He doubled down on not going to a mosque during the interview, but said Muslim Alabamians shouldn’t be worried if he’s elected.
“I love everybody. I love people, but as a Christian man, as one who worships and believes in the Lordship of Jesus Christ, it is the most important thing in my life, and it gives me hope. It anchors me in tough times, and as a Christian man, I’m not going to go to a mosque. I’m not going to do that,” he said. 
Allen said voters should think about who they would trust to be lieutenant governor.
“The voters of this state are going to render a final judgment on June 16 about who they want representing them on the Republican ticket to be a great teammate to Coach (Tommy) Tuberville, and there is nobody else better prepared to step into that role on day one as lieutenant governor and bring all of those relationships, all that experience into that seat (than me),” he said.
Wahl said voters should choose him because of the endorsements he’s gotten from other Republicans who ran for lieutenant governor such as Pat Bishop.
“I’m very proud of those endorsements, and I think it speaks a lot to my values, and the fact that my former opponents see what I stand for, and they put faith in me,” he said.



Meet the Candidates

title: Firefighter, school superintendent seek GOP nod in east Alabama House district
description: Republican voters on Tuesday in Randolph, Chambers and Lee counties will choose their nominee for House District 37 in a primary runoff election. In the May 19 primary, retired firefighter Jeff Monroe got 3,050 votes (38.3%) and Randolph County Superintendent John Jacobs got 2,766 votes (34.7%), according to unofficial returns. A third candidate, Donna Baile[...]
text:
Republican voters on Tuesday in Randolph, Chambers and Lee counties will choose between John Jacobs (left) and Jeff Monroe (right) for their nominee for House District 37 in a primary runoff election. The winner will face Democratic nominee Michelle French in November. (photos courtesy of candidates; graphic by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Republican voters on Tuesday in Randolph, Chambers and Lee counties will choose their nominee for House District 37 in a primary runoff election.
In the May 19 primary, retired firefighter Jeff Monroe got 3,050 votes (38.3%) and Randolph County Superintendent John Jacobs got 2,766 votes (34.7%), according to unofficial returns. A third candidate, Donna Bailey McKay, got 2,149 votes (27%). 
The rural district covers Randolph County and most of Chambers County, and a small portion of northern Lee County. Current Rep. Bob Fincher, R-Woodland, is not seeking reelection after representing the district for 12 years.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In 2018, Fincher got 71.2% of the votes over then-Democratic nominee Charlotte Clark-Frieson, according to election results. In 2014, Fincher got 49.6% of the votes over then-Democratic nominee Josh Burns, who got 46% of the votes, and independent candidate Guy Kelley, who got 4.4% of the votes. The district had a Democratic representative, Richard Laird, from 1974 to 2014, who changed his affiliation to independent in 2013. The winner of Tuesday’s runoff will face Democratic nominee Michelle French, a graphic designer from Roanoke. 
The candidates
Jacobs, 69, said in a phone interview Wednesday that being a state representative is a way for him to spend more time with his family while still contributing to education. He has served as the Randolph County Superintendent for three terms, and was on the county’s school board for one term.
“I think I can make a difference in education and other things, and it seems to be a good fit,” Jacobs said. 
If elected, Jacobs said he wants to focus on education, infrastructure and agriculture. He said that schools should have equal opportunities regardless of their location.
“The rural counties, they don’t have as much tax base and don’t have as much money as the cities do. I’d like to see some way to help the smaller communities solve as possible,” he said. “For technical education, everybody doesn’t have to have a college degree to be successful, and to make a good living.”
He said that voters should choose him because he has worked with lawmakers in Montgomery over the years and understands the process.
“I think that my history with Montgomery gives me a leg up, because I already know the people, the players in Montgomery,” Jacobs said. “I don’t have to have a year to kind of learn what’s going on.”
Monroe, 65, said in a phone interview Wednesday that his career as a firefighter inspired him to run for office. 
“There were times in my career that people totally, 100% trusted and depended on me for their life or their property, either one, but mostly in their life,” Monroe said. “All I’m trying to do is go to Montgomery now and continue serving people.”
If elected, Monroe said public safety, career tech education and rural infrastructure would be his top priorities. He said that while he values higher education, not every student needs one.
“We need tons of tradesmen, we need tons more of highly skilled labor workforce, where it ain’t just a job, but they get a good career,” Monroe said. 
Monroe promised that if voters choose him Tuesday that he will be accountable and transparent and listen to their concerns. 
“People don’t work for me. I am here to serve the public. I served them in my capacity in public safety all my life, and I want to continue to serve,” he said. 
The general election
The winner of the runoff will face French, 66, in November. She said in a phone interview Wednesday that she is running for office because she was “appalled by some of the ridiculous laws coming out of Montgomery.”
If elected, French said her top priority would be to repeal the CHOOSE Act, a voucher-like tax credit that awards up to $7,000 to parents for education-based expenses, including private school tuition, tutoring, educational therapy and school supplies.
“That is damaging to public schools by taking money out of public education and putting it into private schools that do not have to meet the basic standards that public schools do,” French said of the CHOOSE Act.
She promised that if voters choose her in November that she will represent all residents of the district.
“I am going to be there for voters up close and personal. Everybody has an invitation to my front porch, and I will show up where I am asked,” she said.
Campaign fundraising
According to campaign finance records, Jacobs has raised about $81,400 as of Wednesday and spent about $41,000. Most of his contributions (65.7%) come from political action committees (PACs), followed by individuals at 16.8% and businesses at 15%. 
As of Wednesday, Monroe has raised about $136,000 and spent about $97,500, according to campaign finance records. About $78,000 of Monroe’s funds are listed as loans from himself, making up about 57.3% of his funds. About 36.1% of his contributions come from PACs, followed by 2.8% from individuals and 2% from businesses. 
French has raised about $11,200 and spent about $8,700 as of Wednesday, according to campaign finance records. All of her contributions have come from individuals, except for a refund from an Oxford Best Buy. 
How to vote
District 37 voters can choose between Jacobs or Monroe for the Republican nomination on June 16. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Polling locations can be found here. The winner will face French in November in the general election.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Fifty for 150: Denver International Airport, now a top economic driver in Colorado, opens in 1995
description: The first passenger flight took off from Denver International Airport in the early hours of Feb. 28, 1995, in the foggy and snowy conditions the airport is now used to after three decades of operation.  Former Denver Mayor and then-U.S. Secretary of Transportation Federico Peña presented Mayor Wellington Webb with the Federal Aviation Administration operatin[...]
text:
A view of Jeppesen Terminal at Denver International Airport. (Courtesy of Denver International Airport)The first passenger flight took off from Denver International Airport in the early hours of Feb. 28, 1995, in the foggy and snowy conditions the airport is now used to after three decades of operation. 



This story is part of Colorado at 150. Each Fifty for 150 story focuses on an event that helped define Colorado over 150 years of statehood. Newsline is publishing one Fifty for 150 story every weekday in reverse chronological order until the sesquicentennial, Aug. 1, when the final of 50 stories, about the declaration of statehood, will appear.


Former Denver Mayor and then-U.S. Secretary of Transportation Federico Peña presented Mayor Wellington Webb with the Federal Aviation Administration operating certificate the night before, marking the official opening of the airport. 
“It was a great day and it was satisfying to all of us; to many, many people,” Peña told The Denver Post after the airport’s 25th anniversary. “Because, first of all, we had shown the country that Denver, Colorado … could actually do something like this. And, secondly, to all the people that did not believe, who thought it was too much of a risk to do these things, we proved to them that they were wrong.”
DIA at the time became the first airport in the world capable of landing three jets at once with limited visibility. It is located about 25 miles outside of the main city center, which Peña said was intentional to keep the noise that comes with an airport away from established neighborhoods. 
The airport replaced Stapleton International Airport, which operated for more than 65 years in what is now Denver’s Central Park neighborhood. Construction for the new airport kicked off when Peña was mayor at the end of 1989. 
More than 30 years later, Denver’s airport remains the newest major city airport built from scratch in the U.S. 
DIA is set on 53 square miles of land, leaving plenty of room for future growth. Denver annexed the land for the airport from Adams County through intergovernmental agreements that voters from both counties approved. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The opening of DIA was delayed 16 months due to the construction of what was supposed to be an innovative, computerized baggage system to transport luggage between planes and baggage claim. The system, which cost hundreds of millions of dollars to build and maintain, turned out to be a massive failure, damaging bags, directing bags to the wrong destinations, and causing delays despite promises of reducing them. 
Over 1 billion passengers have since traveled through the airport, which is infamous for the plethora of conspiracy theories surrounding art installations, purported underground tunnels and bunkers, secret societies and more. 
Anyone who has driven Peña Boulevard to or from the airport since 2008 is familiar with the menacing 32-foot Blue Mustang sculpture, colloquially known as Blucifer, welcoming travelers with glowing red eyes. The family of artist Luis Jiménez had to finish constructing the sculpture commissioned by the city after a piece of it fell on the artist and killed him.
The Jeppesen Terminal is topped off with DIA’s unique tented roof, designed to resemble Denver’s views of the Rocky Mountains and to let in the copious amounts of natural sunlight in Denver. Right next to the terminal is the Westin Hotel that opened in 2015, shaped to resemble wings. 
The Regional Transportation District opened the A-Line train in 2016 to take passengers from Union Station directly to the airport terminal, a public transportation solution to save travelers the high costs of a long cab ride from the airport. 
In 2025, DIA was the 10th busiest airport in the world and 4th busiest in the U.S., when more than 82 million passengers passed through. The airport, which serves 235 nonstop destinations, is Colorado’s primary economic driver, generating more than $47 billion for the state’s economy annually, according to the airport.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: The final school bell should not be where opportunity ends for Colorado kids
description: Colorado families know that what happens after the last school bell matters as much as what happens before it. The hours between 3 and 6 p.m. — and throughout the summer — are when a child finds a coach, discovers robotics, explores the arts, or comes home to an empty house and a screen. That […]
text:
(Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Colorado families know that what happens after the last school bell matters as much as what happens before it. The hours between 3 and 6 p.m. — and throughout the summer — are when a child finds a coach, discovers robotics, explores the arts, or comes home to an empty house and a screen. That difference has become one of Colorado’s biggest opportunity gaps, and now we have a rare chance to close it.
Like us, Colorado parents know the value of after-school and summer enrichment. These are not nice-to-haves; they’re must-haves for positive youth development. Kids who have trusted adults and supportive peers engage in less risky behavior, have stronger academic outcomes and feel more hopeful about the future.
But we’re also not naive. Simply having this information doesn’t change parents’ abilities to sign their kids up for additional tutoring, soccer or theater camp. Having access to financial resources makes all the difference.
The problem is that these opportunities remain out of reach for too many Colorado kids.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Families in the highest income bracket spend nine times more on enrichment than families in the lowest income bracket. Three out of every four kids who want to participate in an after-school program are missing out. Often these are kids attending public schools. That’s not a choice gap. It’s a geography gap, an access gap and a resource gap.
For years, advocates for afterschool and summer enrichment have explored ways to provide more opportunities to kids from low-income backgrounds. Building on their work, Gary Community Ventures, in partnership with the City and County of Denver and Mile High United Way, decided to test what would happen if parents were given the resources — and the agency — to choose the best opportunities for their kids.
 


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



We gave parents a $1,000 debit card, vetted more than 200 quality providers and let families decide. Known as My Spark, the program helped more than 4,000 Denver middle schoolers pursue their passion, find purpose and develop resilience. A third-party evaluation revealed 8 in 10 kids felt more connected to peers and trusted adults, had higher self-esteem and stronger ties to their neighborhoods.
These insights, when fueled with public dollars invested in our own backyard, could be one of the most valuable ways to support our public school kids outside of the school day. But, we need greater public investment, especially following the recent cuts state lawmakers made to the modest $25 million Colorado allocates to out-of-school programming annually.
While regulations are due this summer, the new federal tax-credit scholarship program could provide an additional funding source to expand after-school and enrichment programming to kids in public schools. Beginning in 2027, taxpayers can donate up to $1,700 to a Scholarship Granting Organization and receive a dollar-for-dollar credit on their federal taxes. Estimates suggest millions could flow into Colorado annually. Gov. Jared Polis made Colorado the first Democratic state to opt in, and he anchored our participation around after-school and summer programs for kids furthest from opportunity.
This opportunity will be defined by what Colorado does next. If we do nothing, we’ll leave precious federal dollars on the table while our kids fall behind those in other states. If we lead, we can expand opportunities for public school kids, build on the choice-driven model My Spark proved over two years, and do it with the community collaboration that has long made our state an outlier in American policymaking.
While some funds may support private school tuition, Colorado also has an opportunity to direct significant resources toward after-school and enrichment programs serving public school students from the Eastern Plains to the Western Slope. We know those concerned about this tax credit share our commitment to helping public school students thrive, and we support this effort only if it advances that goal. We have an unprecedented opportunity to put the well-being of public school kids above adult politics, and we should take it.
But we need partners across philanthropy, education, after-school providers, employers, and policy to come to the table with fresh ideas and questions. We have a proven model. We have the moment. What we need is the will to meet it, together, for the kids who have been waiting the longest.
